title: Third Maximum Number
description: Brute force to optimized: collecting and sorting distinct values versus a single pass maintaining 3 running trackers for the top distinct values.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums, return the third distinct maximum value in the array. If the third distinct maximum does not exist (fewer than 3 distinct values), return the maximum value instead.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Find the third largest distinct value in nums; if there are fewer than 3 distinct values, return the largest one instead.

blocks.title: Analogy: Announcing the Bronze Medalist, Skipping Ties
blocks.text: Picture ranking competitors by score, but ties count as the SAME placement (so two people tied for first still only take up one "slot"), and needing to identify whoever holds third place among distinct scores, or first place if there simply aren't 3 distinct scores.

blocks.caption: Track only the top 3 distinct values seen so far, updated in one pass

blocks.text: The three distinct values are 3, 2, 1; the third largest is 1.
Only 2 distinct values exist, so the maximum, 2, is returned instead.
The distinct values are 3, 2, 1 (the repeated 2 counts once); the third largest is 1.
Before sorting the entire array to find the third distinct value, notice that only 3 running trackers are ever needed: the first, second, and third largest distinct values seen so far.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Only the top 3 distinct values ever matter, everything else in the array can be ignored once it is clear it does not belong in that top 3.

Observation 2: Scanning the array once, maintaining first, second, and third running maximums (each initialized to a sentinel representing "not yet seen"), correctly tracks the top 3 distinct values.

Observation 3: A value equal to one of the current trackers must be skipped entirely, since it is a duplicate, not a new distinct value.

Observation 4: If the third tracker was never updated by the end of the scan, fewer than 3 distinct values exist, and the first tracker (the true maximum) is returned instead.
This leads to a single-pass scan maintaining exactly 3 running "top distinct value" trackers, updating them carefully to skip duplicates.
Collect every distinct value, sort them in descending order, and pick the third one (or the first, if fewer than 3 exist).

items: Build a set of distinct values from nums.
Sort that set in descending order.
Return the third element if it exists, otherwise the first.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: collect distinct values, sort them, pick the third

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every distinct value is collected first, then sorted, before the third one can be selected.
This does more work than necessary, since only the top 3 distinct values are ever actually needed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by sorting the distinct values.
Space: O(n), storing every distinct value.
Limitation: collecting and sorting every distinct value is unnecessary when only the top 3 are ever needed; a single pass with 3 running trackers suffices.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why sorting everything is unnecessary: only 3 values, the current top 3 distinct maximums, ever need to be tracked.

How to update the trackers: for each new value, if it already equals one of the 3 trackers, skip it (duplicate); otherwise, insert it into the correct position among the 3, shifting the others down as needed.

What if fewer than 3 distinct values exist: the third tracker remains at its initial "unseen" sentinel, signaling that the maximum (first tracker) should be returned instead.

The core idea: scan once, maintaining exactly 3 running trackers for the top distinct values, skipping duplicates.

Initialize three trackers, first, second, third, to a sentinel representing "not yet seen." Scan nums once: skip any value equal to one of the trackers; otherwise, insert it into the correct tracker, shifting smaller trackers down. Return the third tracker if it was set, otherwise the first.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: single pass, 3 running trackers, skip duplicates

blocks.text: Maintaining exactly 3 running trackers, and carefully shifting them whenever a genuinely new (non-duplicate) value beats one of them, correctly reproduces the top 3 distinct values without ever sorting or storing the full list. If fewer than 3 distinct values are ever seen, the third tracker simply remains unset, correctly signaling that the maximum should be returned instead.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass.
Space: O(1), just 3 tracker variables.

blocks.text: Third Maximum Number shows that when only a small, FIXED number of top values are needed, tracking that many running variables in a single pass beats sorting or collecting the entire array.

items: Forgetting to skip duplicate values, which would incorrectly treat a repeated value as a new distinct entry.
Using 0 (or another in-range value) as the "not yet seen" sentinel instead of a value guaranteed to never appear (like None, or a value outside the valid input range).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Fewer than 3 distinct values","The maximum value is returned instead."],["Negative numbers present","The sentinel for \"not yet seen\" must not collide with any valid input value."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "track only 3 running values, skip duplicates" as the whole strategy demonstrates the key insight clearly before writing any code.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid sorting the whole array", think: only 3 running trackers are ever needed for the top 3 distinct values.

items: How would you generalize this to find the kth distinct maximum, for an arbitrary k?
How would you handle the sentinel value safely if the input could contain any possible integer value?
Any "track the top k values with fixed, small k" problem, solvable with k running trackers instead of a full sort.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n log n) time and O(n) space. The optimized 3-tracker approach runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.

items: Pattern: tracking a small, fixed number of top distinct values with running variables, in one pass.
Core Idea: maintain first, second, and third running maximums, skipping duplicates, and shifting trackers down when a new distinct value beats one of them.
Time: O(n log n) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, O(1) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: only 3 running trackers are ever needed, no full sort or distinct-value collection required.
Interview Difficulty: a clean, quick problem once duplicate-skipping is handled correctly.
One line memory trick: 3 running trackers, skip duplicates, fall back to the max if fewer than 3 distinct values exist.
